long_en: The village sat at the end of a narrow road that wound through the hills for many miles. In winter the snow closed the pass, and for weeks nobody came or went. The people who lived there did not mind. They had wood for their fires, grain in their barns, and one another for company. Each evening they gathered in the hall beside the church, where the old men played cards and the children listened to stories. The baker brought bread, and the teacher brought her violin. When spring returned and the road opened again, travelers were always surprised by how cheerful everyone seemed. They asked what the secret was, and the villagers only smiled. It was not a secret at all. They had simply learned that a long winter passes more quickly when it is shared, and that a warm room full of friends is worth more than an open road.

My grandfather kept bees for most of his life, and he talked to them every morning as if they were old friends. He told them the news of the family, who was getting married, who had been ill, and who had come home from far away. He believed that bees must always be told the truth, or they would leave the hive and never return. As a child I thought this was only a game, but I followed him through the tall grass anyway, carrying the small tin of smoke. He moved slowly and never wore gloves. The bees walked across his hands without stinging him, and he lifted the frames of honey as gently as if he were turning the pages of a book. When he grew too old to climb the hill, I went in his place. On my first morning alone I stood before the hives and did not know what to say, so I simply told them that he sent his love.

Learning to cook is mostly a matter of paying attention. A recipe can tell you how much salt to add and how long to leave a pot on the stove, but it cannot tell you what your own kitchen smells like when the onions are ready, or how the sound of a pan changes just before the butter begins to burn. Those things you must learn for yourself, one meal at a time. Begin with something simple, such as soup. Cut the vegetables slowly and notice how each one feels under the knife. Taste the broth often, and ask yourself what it needs. Perhaps a little more salt, perhaps a squeeze of lemon, perhaps only more time. Do not be afraid of mistakes, because every cook has made a thousand of them. A soup that is too thin today will teach you how to make a better one tomorrow, and the people at your table will forgive you sooner than you think.

The ferry left the harbor a little after dawn, when the water was still gray and the gulls were only beginning to stir. There were few passengers at that hour. A farmer stood near the rail with two baskets of eggs, and a young woman sat reading a letter that she had clearly read many times before. The captain, who had made this crossing every day for thirty years, leaned out of his window and studied the sky. He did not like the look of the clouds in the west. By the time the island came into view, the wind had risen and the first drops of rain were striking the deck. The farmer covered his baskets with his coat. The young woman folded her letter and put it away. Nobody spoke, but everyone watched the captain, and the captain watched the waves, and slowly and carefully he brought them all safely to the other side.

There is a small shop near the station that repairs watches, and I pass it every day on my way to work. The owner is a quiet man who sits behind the window with a glass held to one eye. I have never seen him look up. Around him hang hundreds of clocks, and no two of them show the same time. For years I wondered why a man who fixes watches would allow such a thing. Last week my own watch stopped, and I finally went inside. While he opened the case with a tiny knife, I asked him about the clocks. He smiled for the first time. Each one, he explained, was set to the hour when its owner first brought it in. Some people never came back, and he could not bring himself to change them. So the shop keeps their time for them, he said, in case they ever return and wish to begin again where they left off.

When the river flooded that spring, the water rose so quickly that the family had only a few minutes to leave the house. The mother carried the baby, the father carried a bag of food, and the two older children each took one thing they could not bear to lose. The boy chose his dog. The girl chose a wooden box that her grandmother had given her, though she had never been told what was inside. They climbed the hill behind the farm and watched the brown water cover the fields, the fence, and at last the kitchen door. They slept that night in a neighbor's barn. In the morning the girl opened the box. Inside she found a handful of seeds wrapped in paper, and a note in her grandmother's careful writing. The note said that a garden can always be planted again. When the water went down, that is exactly what they did.

Good afternoon, and welcome to the city museum. Before we begin our tour, I would like to share a few simple rules. Please do not touch the paintings or lean against the glass cases. You are welcome to take photographs in most rooms, but we ask that you turn off the flash, because bright light can damage the older works. Food and drink are not allowed in the galleries. If you become separated from the group, wait beside the large staircase in the main hall, and a member of staff will help you find us. Our visit today will last about an hour. We will start with the collection of maps on the ground floor, then climb to the gallery of portraits, and finish in the garden, where you may rest for as long as you like. If you have any questions along the way, please do not hesitate to ask. Now, if everyone is ready, let us begin.

My sister and I shared a bedroom until I was fourteen, and for most of those years we fought about everything. We fought about the window, which she wanted open and I wanted closed. We fought about the lamp, the radio, and whose turn it was to sweep the floor. Our mother used to say that she could hear us arguing from the garden. Then one summer my sister went away to study in another city, and the room became mine alone. I opened and closed the window whenever I pleased. I read until midnight with the lamp on. For about a week it was wonderful. After that the room simply felt too quiet, and I found myself writing her long letters about nothing at all. She wrote back the same day. We are both grown now, with houses of our own, but we still speak on the telephone every Sunday, and we have not had a real argument in years.

The first thing you notice about the desert is the silence. There is no traffic, no running water, and on a still day not even the sound of wind. The second thing you notice is the light. At noon it is white and hard, and every stone throws a short black shadow. But in the last hour before sunset the whole land turns the color of honey, and the distant mountains seem close enough to touch. People who visit for the first time often expect the desert to be empty. They are surprised to find tracks in the sand each morning, left by foxes, lizards, and small birds that come out only after dark. If you sit quietly beside a rock and wait, you may see some of them yourself. Bring plenty of water, wear a hat, and tell someone where you are going. The desert is beautiful, but it does not forgive those who forget to respect it.

Every Saturday morning the square in front of the town hall fills with tables, and the weekly market begins. The farmers arrive first, while it is still dark, and set out their apples, cheese, and jars of honey. The fish seller comes next, pushing a cart packed with ice. By eight the square is crowded, and the air smells of fresh bread and coffee. Old friends stop to talk in the middle of the path, and nobody seems to mind. A man with a guitar plays the same three songs he has played for twenty years, and the children dance to them as though they were new. My favorite table belongs to a woman who sells nothing but soup. She makes a different kind each week and never tells anyone what it will be. People wait in a long line to find out. When the church bell rings at noon, the tables are folded, the square is swept, and the town is quiet again until the next Saturday.
